definitions.definition: The amount of time a prediction was made before it was proven true.
definitions.example: If someone in 1800 said 'humans will fly' and it happened in 1903, that's a 103-year predictive lead.

definitions.definition: Based on observation or experience, not just theory.
definitions.example: A doctor testing a medicine on patients is using empirical data.

definitions.definition: The belief that everything can be explained by natural laws and physical things, without needing God or spirits.
definitions.example: A naturalist would say lightning is just electricity, not a god throwing bolts.

definitions.definition: The idea that the universe's settings (like gravity's strength) are perfectly set for life, as if adjusted on purpose.
definitions.example: Like a radio dial that must be exactly on the right station to get clear music.

definitions.definition: A proof that in any logical system, there are true statements that cannot be proven inside that system.
definitions.example: Like a puzzle where some pieces are missing, and you can't prove they're missing from inside the puzzle.

definitions.definition: The mystery of why we have subjective experiences (like feeling pain or seeing red) instead of just processing information.
definitions.example: We know which brain parts light up when you taste chocolate, but not why it feels like something to taste it.

definitions.definition: The surprising fact that abstract math, invented in the mind, perfectly describes the real physical world.
definitions.example: A mathematician invents a new shape for fun, and 50 years later scientists find that shape in nature.

definitions.definition: The universe started in a very ordered, unlikely state, which is strange because things naturally get more disordered over time.
definitions.example: Imagine a deck of cards perfectly sorted by suit and number—that's low entropy. It's much more likely to be shuffled randomly.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to become more disordered over time.
definitions.example: A sandcastle on the beach slowly crumbles into a pile of sand—that's entropy increasing.

definitions.definition: The idea that information (like DNA code) cannot come from nothing; it must be created or sent by something.
definitions.example: A message in a bottle didn't write itself—someone had to put it there.

definitions.definition: A rule that erasing information in a computer creates a tiny amount of heat, showing information is physical.
definitions.example: When you delete a file on your laptop, the computer gets a tiny bit warmer because of the information being erased.

definitions.definition: A mathematical way to measure and understand information, like how much data a message contains or how to send it without errors.
definitions.example: It's why your phone can send a photo without losing all the details.

definitions.definition: Experiments that tested if human thoughts can affect random number generators, suggesting mind-matter interaction.
definitions.example: People trying to 'will' a coin to land on heads more often, and measuring if it actually does.

definitions.definition: Basic starting assumptions that are accepted as true without proof, used to build a system of knowledge.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: Knowledge or truth that God is believed to have shown to humans, often through scripture or direct communication.
definitions.example: Christians believe the Bible is a revelation from God.

definitions.definition: Knowledge of events before they happen; foresight.
definitions.example: If you predict a rainstorm and it happens, that's prescience.

definitions.definition: People who believe only physical matter exists, and everything can be explained by physical laws.
definitions.example: A materialist would say thoughts are just brain chemicals, not a soul.
definitions.first_appearance: Now run it the other direction

definitions.definition: A claim that cannot be proven wrong because there's no way to test it.
definitions.example: Saying 'invisible unicorns live on Mars' is unfalsifiable—you can't prove they don't exist.

definitions.definition: The idea that our universe is just one of many, possibly infinite, universes with different laws and constants.
definitions.example: Like a bubble bath where each bubble is a separate universe with its own rules.

definitions.definition: A set of symbols and rules for manipulating them, used in logic and math to prove statements.
definitions.example: Chess is a formal system: pieces (symbols) and rules for moving them.

definitions.definition: Being able to prove or justify itself using only its own rules, without needing anything outside.
definitions.example: A dictionary that defines every word using only words from the same dictionary—it might be circular.

definitions.definition: The specific brain activities that happen at the same time as a mental experience, like seeing a color.
definitions.example: When you feel happy, certain brain areas light up on a scan—those are neural correlates of happiness.

definitions.definition: A type of geometry where the usual rules (like parallel lines never meeting) are changed, used to describe curved space.
definitions.example: On a globe, lines of longitude are parallel at the equator but meet at the poles—that's non-Euclidean.

definitions.definition: A branch of math that studies symmetry and the ways things can be combined or transformed.
definitions.example: It explains why a snowflake has six identical sides—it's about symmetry.

definitions.definition: The best scientific theory that describes all the known fundamental particles and how they interact.
definitions.example: It's like a periodic table for the smallest building blocks of matter.

definitions.definition: Matter made of particles opposite to normal matter (like opposite charge); when they meet, they destroy each other in a burst of energy.
definitions.example: In sci-fi, starship engines sometimes use matter-antimatter reactions for power.

definitions.definition: Related to heat, energy, and how they move and change in physical systems.
definitions.example: A steam engine uses thermodynamic principles to turn heat into motion.

definitions.definition: The pairs of chemicals (A-T and C-G) that form the rungs of the DNA ladder, carrying genetic information.
definitions.example: Like letters in a code: A, T, C, G pair up to spell out instructions for building a living thing.

definitions.definition: The property of something that cannot be simplified or broken down into smaller parts.
definitions.example: A mousetrap is irreducible—if you remove one piece, it won't work at all.

definitions.definition: The process of different things coming together to the same point or conclusion.
definitions.example: Two friends walking from different houses to the same school is convergence.

definitions.definition: A result that is unlikely to be due to chance, so it's probably real.
definitions.example: If you flip a coin 100 times and get 95 heads, that's statistically significant—it's not just luck.

definitions.definition: A measure of how sure scientists are about a result; higher sigma means more certainty (7 sigma is extremely certain).
definitions.example: A 5-sigma result is considered a discovery in physics; 7-sigma is even stronger.

definitions.definition: The idea that every physical event has a physical cause, and nothing outside the physical world can affect it.
definitions.example: If you believe in causal closure, you'd say a prayer can't make a sick person better—only medicine can.
definitions.first_appearance: Not 'the system hasn't found the answer yet'
